barkcloth.origin: Barkcloth is a nonwoven sheet made from the inner bark (phloem) of trees in the mulberry family (Moraceae) and related plants. In the Pacific the main source is paper mulberry, Broussonetia papyrifera, a dioecious East Asian tree carried into Oceania as a clonally propagated crop; other species, including some endemic to Hawaii and New Zealand, were also used. In Uganda, traditional bark cloth is made from Ficus natalensis. Pacific names include tapa, siapo (Samoa) and kapa (Hawaii).
barkcloth.structure: Barkcloth consists of long phloem fibers and their surrounding tissue, felted and interlocked by beating rather than spun or woven. The fibers are cellulosic with modest lignin; paper mulberry has a high ratio of syringyl to guaiacyl lignin units, which is thought to aid pulping and beating. Beating spreads and thins the bast into a sheet whose fibers run in overlapping directions, and separate pieces can be joined into larger cloths. The result is a paper-like material whose strength and drape depend on bark quality and beating.
barkcloth.process: In Oceania, paper mulberry is grown as coppiced shoots that are harvested before flowering. The bark is removed from the stems and the inner bast is separated from the outer bark, soaked and beaten with wooden beaters until it spreads into a thin, wide sheet. Beaten pieces are dried and joined into larger cloths, which are then decorated by painting, printing or dyeing with plant colorants and mineral pigments. Methods, tools and designs differ among island groups. In Uganda, bark cloth from Ficus natalensis is still made by traditional methods, and the finished cloth has been studied for possible wound-care uses.
barkcloth.performance: Barkcloth is light and can be supple or papery, but like paper it has limited wet strength and abrasion resistance, so it is not laundered like woven cloth. Museum pieces need controlled humidity and protection from light, insects and mold. Pacific colorants identified on historic cloths include noni (morindin and morindone), turmeric, tree tannins and iron oxide, while mati red in Tahiti combines Cordia subcordata leaves and Ficus tinctoria fruits. Ugandan Ficus bark cloth has shown antimicrobial activity against MRSA in laboratory tests.
barkcloth.identify: Burn tests are indicative only and inappropriate for heritage objects. Barkcloth is recognized by its nonwoven, felted structure with visible beater marks and no yarns. Species identification of historic tapa has used DNA: nuclear ITS-1, microsatellites and chloroplast markers such as the trnL P6 loop, the last usually resolving only to genus. HPLC and portable XRF identify dyes and pigments. Modern imitations may be printed paper or nonwoven synthetics.
barkcloth.labeling: Barkcloth is not a textile fiber under the generic-name lists: Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 has no Annex I name for bark fibers, and US Textile Fiber Products Identification Act rules (16 CFR Part 303) were written around fibers and yarns, so how a given barkcloth product is labeled should be checked case by case. More important are cultural and legal issues: objects may be subject to cultural heritage export laws of the country of origin, and museums increasingly work with source communities on provenance.
barkcloth.past: Genetic studies show that Pacific paper mulberry descends mainly from female clones introduced from Taiwan by Austronesian-speaking voyagers over roughly the last 5,000 years, supporting the out of Taiwan model; nearly all Pacific plants are female except in Hawaii, where male plants are thought to reflect a later introduction by Japanese or Chinese immigrants. Barkcloth is described as a practical and symbolic component of Austronesian cultures, and Western explorers collected many decorated cloths in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, which now allow dye and DNA studies. Samoan siapo remains a living tradition, as does Ugandan bark cloth.
facts: from Taiwan, within roughly the last 5,000 years
beaten, felted nonwoven sheet; no yarns

lotus.origin: Lotus fiber is drawn from the stems of the sacred lotus, Nelumbo nucifera (Nelumbonaceae), an aquatic plant of South and East Asia. The best-documented craft production is widely reported from Myanmar, particularly around Inle Lake; this pass could not verify production volumes, villages, cooperatives or production elsewhere. Output is tiny because each stem yields only a trace of fiber, and it is gathered and processed entirely by hand.
lotus.structure: When a lotus stem or root is snapped and pulled apart, fine threads stretch between the pieces. Researchers studying lotus-root fibers describe them as naturally helical microstructures and have even used them as templates for magnetic microswimmers. The strands are extremely fine, cellulosic and initially moist. Detailed, independently published data on the composition, diameter and tensile properties of textile lotus yarn are scarce, so any specification should be requested from the producer.
lotus.process: Craft descriptions, which this pass could not verify against primary sources, say that fresh stems are cut, bundled and snapped at short intervals; the fine filaments drawn out from several stems at once are rolled together on a wet surface into a continuous thread, which is then spun or twisted, reeled, washed and woven, often within a day or two of harvest because stems dry and the strands become unusable. Because verified technical descriptions are limited, workshop claims about quantities of stems per scarf or processing times should be treated as producer statements.
lotus.performance: Lotus cloth is described by makers as light, soft and breathable, with a slightly uneven, linen-like texture; independent laboratory data on strength, abrasion, moisture regain or colorfastness are not readily available. As a cellulosic material it can be expected to burn, absorb water and take direct and reactive dyes, but those expectations should be confirmed by testing. Because the yarn is fine and handmade, fabrics are delicate and are usually washed gently by hand.
lotus.identify: Burn tests are indicative only: a pure lotus yarn should burn like other cellulosics, but many lotus products are blends with silk or cotton. Microscopy may show the helical structures characteristic of lotus strands, which distinguishes them from bast fibers such as linen. Because lotus fiber is expensive and scarce, mislabeling is a real risk; buyers should ask for fiber-content testing and for documentation of the workshop, and should treat unusually low prices with suspicion.
lotus.labeling: Lotus fiber has no Annex I name in Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011, so EU labels would generally declare it as other fibres with its percentage, with silk or cotton blends named separately. In the US, covered textiles must disclose fiber content under the Textile Fiber Products Identification Act (15 U.S.C. 70 et seq.) and 16 CFR Part 303, and the term lotus should not be used for fabrics that merely have a lotus-like finish or print. No certification scheme specific to lotus fiber was identified.
lotus.past: Lotus-stem weaving is associated with Buddhist devotional practice in Myanmar, where lotus cloth has been made for robes offered to revered monks and images, according to widely published accounts that this pass could not verify against primary sources. In recent decades lotus scarves have been marketed to tourists and to luxury buyers. The history of any particular product should therefore be connected to a named workshop rather than assumed.
